newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - From the Beehive - The inscrutable Peters.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - From the Beehive - The inscrutable Peters.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Oct 15 - Prime Minister Jim Bolger may still be cherishing the notion of doing a deal with power broker Winston Peters and NZ First -- but two of his colleagues have rubbished the idea.

Tourism Minister John Banks who just held on to his seat by 196 votes says bluntly Labour will lead the next government: he has no doubt Labour leader Helen Clark will become Prime Minister and Peters deputy prime minister.
And retiring Trade Negotiations Minister Philip Burdon says any deal with Peters would be a "sell-out" by National.

Peters remains inscrutable on his intentions, and his deputy Tau Henare, who just three weeks ago was adamant he could not serve in a National-led coalition with Jim Bolger or Bill Birch, has changed tack and says he would abide by any decision his caucus made.
The NZ First leader arrived back in Wellington yesterday afternoon to assume his anointed role of power broker.
It is expected the NZ First caucus will authorise him to open lines of negotiation with both Labour and National.
He has played brinkmanship all his political life. His ambition to be prime minister has never been hidden from associates.
Peters must extract maximum leverage from being the kingmaker -- though with just 13 percent of the vote, his mandate has a use-it-or-lose-it clause.
If his price is too high, or if he vacillates too long, not only his own constituency but the larger one of the country at large will soon lose patience.
At some point he needs a big trophy to wave before his supporters. Just being deputy prime minister might not be sufficient. He might throw the dice to take on the Finance portfolio.

That's what some of his close advisers believe is the objective NZ First must target if it is to exercise real power inside a Labour-led coalition. But it's a price that Labour could not afford to meet.

Among the public service mandarins of Treasury and Foreign Affairs, there is some alarm that Winston Peters could end up either as Minister of Economic Development (if Labour carries out its threat to split Treasury into two departments) or as Minister of Foreign Affairs.

Meanwhile, there is the conundrum of his Maori Support base. Maori voters swept out Labour MPs, and the question is whether in rejecting Labour last Saturday, they would happily contemplate NZ First joining forces with the party they feel has betrayed them.
At least two of the new Maori MPs had links at one time to the National Party.
Labour's caucus meeting in Wellington spent some time exploring with outgoing Maori MPs the reasons that lay behind the mass desertion by Maori voters.
It seems the party intends to make a major effort to regain its hold on Maoridom, and sees a good base still in the support it gained on the party vote.
Inevitably, in targeting again the Maori seats, it could come into collision with NZ First.
But both could lose ground among white New Zealanders if a Labour-led coalition goes too far in appeasing the Maori vote.
Meanwhile, National has begun the post-mortems on what even some of its own MPs conceded was a dismal campaign.
In some quarters what is euphemistically called a "regeneration" process has begun.

Hints are being carefully dropped that this should start at the top. But the difficulty is that if a Labour-led coalition proves unstable, or could not put together a budget acceptable to both the Alliance and NZ First, then the country could be forced into another election inside the next 12 months.
So national, it's said, needs to retain its present leadership.

But National's key strategists are aware that if the party is to rebuild its image and grow its support base back to the 40 percent essential to lead the right-of-centre parties back into office, then most of the current front-bench will have to make way for new faces inside 18 months.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
